diseases.summary: A common fungal disease that starts on older, lower leaves and moves upward, reducing yield and exposing fruit to sunscald.
symptoms: Brown spots with dark concentric rings (a 'target' or bull's-eye pattern).
Yellow halo around the spots; affected lower leaves turn yellow and drop.
Dark, sunken lesions on stems near the soil line and on the fruit stem end.
diseases.favourableConditions: Warm (24–29 °C), humid weather with long periods of leaf wetness from dew, rain or overhead irrigation.
organicTreatment: Remove and destroy infected lower leaves; do not compost them.
Mulch around plants to stop soil splashing onto leaves.
Spray a neem-oil or Bacillus subtilis based bio-fungicide at the first signs.
chemicalTreatment: A protectant fungicide recommended by the DOA (e.g. mancozeb or chlorothalonil based), following label rates and pre-harvest intervals.
prevention: Rotate with non-solanaceous crops for at least 2 seasons.
Stake and prune plants to improve air flow.
Use certified disease-free seed and resistant varieties where available.

diseases.summary: A fast, destructive water-mould disease that can wipe out a tomato or potato field within days in cool, wet weather.
symptoms: Large, pale-green to dark-brown water-soaked patches on leaves.
White fuzzy growth on the underside of leaves in humid mornings.
Firm, greasy brown blotches on fruit; stems turn black.
diseases.favourableConditions: Cool to mild temperatures (10–25 °C) with very high humidity (above 90 %) or rain for 10 hours or more.
organicTreatment: Remove and bag infected plants immediately to slow spread.
Avoid overhead watering; water early in the day.
Increase spacing and pruning to dry the canopy.
chemicalTreatment: A systemic + protectant fungicide recommended by the DOA for late blight, applied preventively when weather is favourable. Follow the label strictly.
prevention: Plant in well-drained beds with good air movement.
Never leave volunteer potato or tomato plants in the field.
Check the KolaCare risk card daily during rainy spells.

diseases.summary: A fungal disease of humid, poorly ventilated crops — common in polytunnels and dense plantings.
symptoms: Pale green to yellow patches on the upper leaf surface.
Olive-green to brown velvety mould directly beneath on the underside.
Leaves curl, wither and drop; flowers may fail.
diseases.favourableConditions: Relative humidity above 85 % with temperatures of 20–25 °C, especially in protected cultivation.
organicTreatment: Improve ventilation; open tunnel sides during the day.
Remove the lowest leaves and infected foliage.
Avoid wetting leaves when irrigating.
chemicalTreatment: A protectant fungicide recommended by the DOA (e.g. mancozeb or chlorothalonil based), following label rates and pre-harvest intervals.

diseases.summary: A leaf-spotting fungus that defoliates plants from the bottom up during wet weather.
symptoms: Many small circular spots with dark borders and grey-white centres.
Tiny black dots (fruiting bodies) visible in the spot centres.
Heavily spotted leaves yellow and fall off.
diseases.favourableConditions: Warm, wet weather (16–28 °C) with frequent rain splash.
organicTreatment: Remove infected leaves and crop debris.
Mulch the soil surface.
Apply a Bacillus-based bio-fungicide early.
chemicalTreatment: A protectant fungicide recommended by the DOA (e.g. mancozeb or chlorothalonil based), following label rates and pre-harvest intervals.

diseases.summary: A bacterial disease spread by rain splash, tools and seed; it marks fruit and reduces market value.
symptoms: Small, dark, greasy-looking spots on leaves, often with a yellow halo.
Spots merge and leaves look scorched or ragged.
Raised scabby spots on green fruit.
diseases.favourableConditions: Warm (24–32 °C), rainy and windy weather.
organicTreatment: Remove and destroy infected plants and debris.
Disinfect pruning tools between plants.
Avoid handling plants when wet.
chemicalTreatment: Copper-based fungicide/bactericide, used strictly as per the label and DOA recommendations.
prevention: Use certified, pathogen-free seed and seedlings.
Use drip irrigation instead of sprinklers.

diseases.summary: A whitefly-spread virus that stunts plants and can cause near-total yield loss if infection happens early.
symptoms: Upward curling and cupping of young leaves.
Yellow leaf margins and small, crumpled leaves.
Stunted, bushy plants with flower drop.
diseases.favourableConditions: Hot, dry periods when whitefly populations build up.
organicTreatment: Uproot and destroy infected plants early.
Use yellow sticky traps to monitor whiteflies.
Grow seedlings under insect-proof net.
chemicalTreatment: Whitefly control with an insecticide recommended by the DOA, rotating modes of action. The virus itself cannot be cured.
prevention: Remove weed hosts around the field.
Avoid planting next to infected older crops.

diseases.summary: A very stable virus spread by hands, tools and seed; it reduces vigour and fruit quality.
symptoms: Light- and dark-green mottled (mosaic) pattern on leaves.
Fern-like, distorted young leaves.
Uneven ripening and internal browning of fruit.
diseases.favourableConditions: Spread mechanically at any temperature, especially during pruning and handling.
organicTreatment: Remove infected plants.
Wash hands with soap and disinfect tools before handling plants.
Do not smoke or handle tobacco near plants.
chemicalTreatment: No chemical cure. Focus on sanitation and resistant varieties.
prevention: Use resistant varieties and certified seed.

diseases.summary: Tiny sap-sucking mites that thrive in hot, dry conditions and can bronze an entire crop.
symptoms: Fine yellow or white speckling (stippling) on leaves.
Fine webbing on the underside of leaves.
Leaves turn bronze, dry out and drop.
diseases.favourableConditions: Hot (27 °C and above), dry weather with low humidity.
organicTreatment: Spray the underside of leaves with a strong jet of water.
Apply neem-oil or insecticidal soap.
Conserve predatory mites by avoiding broad-spectrum sprays.
chemicalTreatment: A miticide recommended by the DOA, rotating active ingredients to avoid resistance.
prevention: Keep plants well watered to reduce stress.
Inspect the underside of leaves weekly in dry weather.

diseases.summary: A fungal leaf, stem and fruit disease of warm, humid tropical regions.
symptoms: Brown spots with light-brown centres and faint concentric rings.
Spots enlarge and merge, causing leaf collapse.
Small sunken spots on fruit.
diseases.favourableConditions: Warm (20–32 °C) and humid weather with long dew periods.
organicTreatment: Remove lower infected leaves.
Improve air flow by pruning and staking.
chemicalTreatment: A protectant fungicide recommended by the DOA (e.g. mancozeb or chlorothalonil based), following label rates and pre-harvest intervals.

diseases.summary: No disease symptoms detected on this tomato leaf.
symptoms: Uniform green colour.
No spots, mould, curling or webbing.
organicTreatment: No treatment needed. Keep monitoring weekly, especially after rain.
prevention: Scan a few leaves every week to catch problems early.
Water at the base of the plant in the morning so leaves dry quickly.
Keep the field free of weeds and crop debris.

diseases.summary: Fungal leaf spot that weakens potato plants late in the season and reduces tuber size.
symptoms: Dark brown spots with concentric rings on older leaves.
Yellowing around the spots.
Shallow dark lesions on tubers.
diseases.favourableConditions: Alternating wet and dry periods with warm temperatures (18–30 °C).
organicTreatment: Remove infected leaves.
Maintain good soil fertility — stressed plants are more susceptible.
Apply a bio-fungicide at first symptoms.
chemicalTreatment: A protectant fungicide recommended by the DOA (e.g. mancozeb or chlorothalonil based), following label rates and pre-harvest intervals.

diseases.summary: The disease behind the Irish potato famine — still the most serious potato disease in cool, wet up-country areas.
symptoms: Water-soaked, rapidly expanding dark lesions on leaves.
White mould on the leaf underside in humid conditions.
Reddish-brown dry rot inside tubers.
diseases.favourableConditions: Cool (10–25 °C) and very humid weather (above 90 % RH) for 10 hours or more.
organicTreatment: Remove infected plants and volunteer potatoes.
Earth up tubers well so spores cannot reach them.
Avoid irrigating late in the day.
chemicalTreatment: A late-blight fungicide programme recommended by the DOA, started preventively when risk is high.
prevention: Follow the KolaCare risk card during the Maha season.

diseases.summary: No disease symptoms detected on this potato leaf.
symptoms: Uniform green colour.
No spots, lesions or mould.
organicTreatment: No treatment needed. Keep monitoring weekly, especially after rain.
prevention: Scan a few leaves every week to catch problems early.
Water at the base of the plant in the morning so leaves dry quickly.
Keep the field free of weeds and crop debris.

diseases.summary: Bacterial leaf and fruit spot of chilli and capsicum, spread by rain splash and infected seed.
symptoms: Small water-soaked spots that turn brown with a yellow halo.
Leaves yellow and drop, exposing fruit.
Raised, scabby spots on fruit.
diseases.favourableConditions: Warm (24–32 °C), wet and windy weather.
organicTreatment: Remove infected leaves and fruit.
Disinfect tools.
Avoid overhead irrigation.
chemicalTreatment: Copper-based fungicide/bactericide, used strictly as per the label and DOA recommendations.
prevention: Use clean seed and healthy seedlings.

diseases.pathogen: Chilli leaf curl virus complex (whitefly-transmitted), often with thrips/mite damage
diseases.summary: The most damaging problem of chilli in Sri Lanka, caused by viruses spread by whiteflies together with thrips and mites.
symptoms: Leaves curl upward or downward and become small and thick.
Shortened internodes giving a bushy appearance.
Flower drop and very few fruits.
diseases.favourableConditions: Hot, dry weather when vector insects multiply.
organicTreatment: Uproot and destroy infected plants early.
Raise seedlings under insect-proof nets.
Use yellow and blue sticky traps; spray neem-based products.
chemicalTreatment: Vector control with insecticides/miticides recommended by the DOA. The virus itself cannot be cured.
prevention: Grow a border crop such as maize to reduce vector entry.
Avoid planting near older infected crops.

diseases.summary: A fungal fruit rot that causes large post-harvest losses of chilli in humid weather.
symptoms: Sunken, circular, water-soaked spots on ripe fruit.
Concentric rings of black dots or orange spore masses.
Die-back of twigs from the tip.
diseases.favourableConditions: Warm (20–30 °C) and wet weather near harvest.
organicTreatment: Pick and destroy infected fruit.
Dry harvested chilli quickly and hygienically.
chemicalTreatment: A protectant fungicide recommended by the DOA (e.g. mancozeb or chlorothalonil based), following label rates and pre-harvest intervals.

diseases.summary: No disease symptoms detected on this chilli leaf.
symptoms: Uniform green colour.
Flat leaves without curling or spots.
organicTreatment: No treatment needed. Keep monitoring weekly, especially after rain.
prevention: Scan a few leaves every week to catch problems early.
Water at the base of the plant in the morning so leaves dry quickly.
Keep the field free of weeds and crop debris.

diseases.summary: Rust fungus producing powdery pustules on maize leaves; severe infections reduce grain fill.
symptoms: Small, oval, cinnamon-brown powdery pustules on both leaf surfaces.
Pustules turn dark brown to black later in the season.
Heavily infected leaves dry out.
diseases.favourableConditions: Moderate temperatures (16–25 °C) with heavy dew or high humidity.
organicTreatment: Remove heavily infected lower leaves.
Plant early to escape peak infection.
chemicalTreatment: A protectant fungicide recommended by the DOA (e.g. mancozeb or chlorothalonil based), following label rates and pre-harvest intervals.

diseases.summary: A fungal disease producing long grey-green lesions; early infection can cause major yield loss.
symptoms: Long (2.5–15 cm), cigar-shaped grey-green to tan lesions.
Lesions start on lower leaves and move up.
Dark spore masses in lesions during humid weather.
diseases.favourableConditions: Moderate temperatures (18–27 °C) with long dew periods.
organicTreatment: Remove infected debris after harvest.
Ensure balanced fertilisation.
chemicalTreatment: A protectant fungicide recommended by the DOA (e.g. mancozeb or chlorothalonil based), following label rates and pre-harvest intervals.

diseases.summary: A fungal leaf spot favoured by warm, humid weather and maize-on-maize cropping.
symptoms: Narrow, rectangular grey to tan lesions bounded by leaf veins.
Lesions merge and blight whole leaves.
Premature leaf death.
diseases.favourableConditions: Warm (22–30 °C), very humid weather with long periods of leaf wetness.
organicTreatment: Remove infected residues.
Improve field drainage and spacing.
chemicalTreatment: A protectant fungicide recommended by the DOA (e.g. mancozeb or chlorothalonil based), following label rates and pre-harvest intervals.

diseases.summary: An invasive caterpillar pest that has spread across Sri Lanka since 2018 and attacks maize whorls.
symptoms: Ragged holes and 'windowpane' feeding on young leaves.
Sawdust-like droppings (frass) in the whorl.
Caterpillars with an inverted 'Y' mark on the head.
diseases.favourableConditions: Warm weather throughout the year; outbreaks after dry spells.
organicTreatment: Hand-pick egg masses and larvae.
Apply sand–lime or wood ash mixture into the whorl.
Encourage natural enemies.
chemicalTreatment: An insecticide recommended by the DOA for fall armyworm, applied into the whorl when larvae are small.
prevention: Scout fields twice a week for the first 6 weeks.

diseases.summary: No disease symptoms detected on this maize leaf.
symptoms: Uniform green colour.
No lesions, pustules or feeding damage.
organicTreatment: No treatment needed. Keep monitoring weekly, especially after rain.
prevention: Scan a few leaves every week to catch problems early.
Water at the base of the plant in the morning so leaves dry quickly.
Keep the field free of weeds and crop debris.

diseases.summary: The most destructive rice disease worldwide; it attacks leaves, nodes and panicle necks.
symptoms: Diamond (spindle) shaped spots with grey centres and brown borders.
Lesions merge and leaves dry out ('burnt' appearance).
Neck rot causing white, empty panicles.
diseases.favourableConditions: Temperatures of 20–28 °C with long dew periods and high humidity; excess nitrogen increases risk.
organicTreatment: Avoid excessive nitrogen; split fertiliser applications.
Keep fields flooded where possible.
Burn or remove infected straw.
chemicalTreatment: A blast fungicide recommended by the Rice Research and Development Institute (RRDI), applied at early symptoms or booting.
prevention: Grow resistant varieties recommended for your district.

diseases.summary: A fungal disease linked to nutrient-poor soils and water stress; it lowers grain quality.
symptoms: Oval brown spots with grey centres, like sesame seeds.
Spots on grains turn them dark and discoloured.
Seedling blight in severe cases.
diseases.favourableConditions: Warm (25–30 °C), humid weather on poor or drought-stressed soils.
organicTreatment: Correct soil nutrition, especially potassium and silicon.
Maintain proper water levels.
chemicalTreatment: A protectant fungicide recommended by the DOA (e.g. mancozeb or chlorothalonil based), following label rates and pre-harvest intervals.

diseases.summary: A bacterial disease spread through irrigation water and storms; common after floods.
symptoms: Wavy yellow to white stripes starting from the leaf tips and edges.
Leaves wilt and roll (kresek) in young plants.
Milky bacterial ooze on leaves in the morning.
diseases.favourableConditions: Warm (25–34 °C), wet and windy weather, especially after flooding.
organicTreatment: Drain the field periodically.
Avoid excess nitrogen.
Remove infected stubble and weeds.
chemicalTreatment: No highly effective chemical control; follow RRDI advice.
prevention: Avoid clipping seedling tips at transplanting.

diseases.summary: No disease symptoms detected on this rice leaf.
symptoms: Uniform green colour.
No spots, stripes or drying tips.
organicTreatment: No treatment needed. Keep monitoring weekly, especially after rain.
prevention: Scan a few leaves every week to catch problems early.
Water at the base of the plant in the morning so leaves dry quickly.
Keep the field free of weeds and crop debris.

diseases.summary: Colour analysis found no significant yellowing or dead tissue on this leaf.
symptoms: Mostly uniform green leaf tissue.
organicTreatment: No treatment needed. Keep monitoring weekly, especially after rain.
prevention: Scan a few leaves every week to catch problems early.
Water at the base of the plant in the morning so leaves dry quickly.
Keep the field free of weeds and crop debris.

diseases.pathogen: Likely fungal or bacterial leaf spot
diseases.summary: Colour analysis found dead (brown/black) tissue typical of fungal or bacterial leaf spots and blights. Compare with the crop-specific guides in the Library.
symptoms: Brown or black spots or patches on the leaf.
Possible yellow halo around spots.
diseases.favourableConditions: Usually favoured by warm, wet weather and leaf wetness.
organicTreatment: Remove and destroy affected leaves.
Avoid overhead watering and improve air flow.
Re-scan in a few days to see if the spots are spreading.
chemicalTreatment: If spots spread quickly, consult your Agriculture Instructor or the 1920 call centre before spraying.
prevention: Rotate crops and remove crop debris.

diseases.pathogen: Nutrient deficiency, root stress or early viral infection
diseases.summary: Colour analysis found yellowing leaf tissue. This can be a nutrient deficiency (often nitrogen, magnesium or iron), waterlogging, or an early virus symptom.
symptoms: Pale or yellow areas on the leaf.
Older leaves yellowing first suggests nitrogen or magnesium shortage.
diseases.favourableConditions: Waterlogged or poor soils, long dry spells, or insect vectors.
organicTreatment: Check soil moisture and drainage.
Apply compost or a balanced fertiliser based on a soil test.
Look under leaves for whiteflies, aphids or mites.
chemicalTreatment: Use fertiliser as recommended by the DOA for your crop and soil.
